Organic farming grows crops using compost, green manure, crop rotation and natural pest control instead of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides. It keeps the soil alive, protects water and gives farmers food that is safer to eat.

For our Community Service Project we set up a small organic plot, prepared compost and vermicompost, sowed seeds, used neem-based sprays against pests and recorded what happened every week.

Our aim was simple: show that a low-cost, chemical-free method can work for small farmers, and share that message with the people around us.

Key observations from our work. Add your own measurements and results here.

Soil health first

Compost and vermicompost add nutrients and organic matter, so the soil holds water and feeds plants for longer.

Better water use

Mulching and humus-rich soil reduce evaporation, so the plot needed less frequent watering.

Lower input cost

Kitchen waste, cow dung and neem leaves replace bought chemicals, which matters most for small farmers.

Safer food

No synthetic pesticide residue on vegetables means safer food for families and for the farmers who handle it.

Natural pest control

Neem spray, companion plants and healthy soil kept pests down without harming useful insects like bees and earthworms.

A closed loop

Crop residue and kitchen waste go back into compost, so very little leaves the farm as waste.

AspectOrganic methodChemical method
FertilizerCompost, vermicompost, green manureSynthetic NPK fertilizers
Pest controlNeem, crop rotation, companion plantsSynthetic pesticides
Soil over timeGets richer and holds more waterCan lose organic matter
Nearby waterLow runoff of chemicalsRunoff can pollute water

What the team did in each week. Edit the details to match your own record.

  1. WEEK1
    Plan

    Planning and team setup

    Chose the topic, formed the team of five, divided roles and read about organic methods.

  2. WEEK2
    Survey

    Survey and site selection

    Talked to local farmers about chemical use and picked a plot for the project.

  3. WEEK3
    Prepare

    Soil preparation

    Cleared and tilled the plot, checked the soil and marked out the beds.

  4. WEEK4
    Compost

    Compost and bio-fertilizer

    Prepared compost and vermicompost and applied them to the beds.

  5. WEEK5
    Sow

    Sowing seeds

    Sowed the chosen crops, mulched the beds and started a watering routine.

  6. WEEK6
    Protect

    Natural pest control

    Made and sprayed neem solution, removed weeds by hand and noted any pest attacks.

  7. WEEK7
    Measure

    Monitoring and growth records

    Measured plant growth, photographed the plot and compared it with notes from the farmers.

  8. WEEK8
    Harvest

    Harvest, report and awareness

    Harvested the crop, wrote the final report and shared the results with the community.

Organic farming is practical, affordable and kind to the land. Eight weeks of work on a small plot gave us a clear picture of how it can help farmers and the environment.

It works at small scale

A student team with simple tools and local materials was enough to run a healthy organic plot.

The soil improves

Regular compost kept the soil loose, moist and full of life.

Awareness matters

Sharing what we learned with farmers and neighbours is how the practice spreads.
